prompt: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve that HTTP/1.1 keep-alive does not?

options.text: HTTP/2 encrypts traffic; HTTP/1.1 does not
HTTP/2 allows multiple request–response streams on one connection without waiting for each to complete
HTTP/2 uses UDP instead of TCP
HTTP/2 compresses response bodies; HTTP/1.1 does not

explanation: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a connection but still processes one request at a time (serial). HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent streams on one connection. (a) Both versions can use TLS. (c) HTTP/2 uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. (d) Both versions support body compression via Content-Encoding.

prompt: Why does HTTP/3 use QUIC (over UDP) instead of TCP?

options.text: UDP is more reliable than TCP
QUIC provides per-stream reliability, eliminating TCP-level head-of-line blocking
TCP does not support encryption
UDP is required for binary protocols

explanation: TCP enforces ordering across the entire connection; one lost packet blocks all streams. QUIC handles reliability per stream, so a loss on one stream does not affect others. (a) UDP itself is unreliable; QUIC adds reliability on top. (c) TCP supports TLS just fine. (d) There is no such requirement.

prompt: Which HTTP method is both **safe** and **idempotent**?

options.text: POST
PUT
GET
DELETE

explanation: GET does not change server state (safe) and repeating it gives the same result (idempotent). (a) POST is neither safe nor idempotent. (b) PUT is idempotent but not safe (it changes the resource). (d) DELETE is idempotent but not safe.

prompt: What does it mean for PUT to be **idempotent**?

options.text: PUT requests are always successful
Sending the same PUT request multiple times has the same effect as sending it once
PUT requests do not change server state
PUT requests cannot be cached

explanation: Idempotent means the result is the same whether you send the request once or many times. The first PUT sets the resource; subsequent identical PUTs set it to the same value. (a) PUT can fail with 4xx or 5xx. (c) PUT does change state; it is not safe. (d) Cacheability is separate from idempotency.

prompt: A client receives a `304 Not Modified` response. What does this mean?

options.text: The resource does not exist
The resource has not changed since the client's last request; use the cached version
The server encountered an error
The request was redirected to a different URL

explanation: 304 is returned when a conditional request (If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since) shows the content has not changed. The server sends no body, saving bandwidth. (a) That is 404. (c) Server errors are 5xx. (d) Redirects are 3xx but specifically 301, 302, 307, 308.

prompt: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Cache-Control: no-store`?

options.text: They are identical
no-cache caches the response but revalidates on every use; no-store prevents caching entirely
no-cache prevents caching; no-store allows caching with revalidation
no-cache applies to browsers; no-store applies to CDNs

explanation: no-cache stores the response but requires the client to check with the origin before using it (via conditional request). no-store means do not store the response at all. (a) and (c) confuse the two. (d) Both apply to any cache.

scenario: Your API has a POST /orders endpoint. A client sends an order but gets a network timeout and does not know if the server received it.
prompt: How should the system handle retries safely?

options.text: The client retries the same POST; duplicate orders are acceptable
The client includes an idempotency key with each request. The server checks the key and returns the original response if it has already processed that key.
Change POST to GET so retries are safe
Never retry; show an error and make the user re-enter the order

explanation: An idempotency key lets the server detect duplicate requests and return the same response without processing the order twice. (a) Duplicate orders are a business problem. (c) GET is for retrieval, not creation. (d) Poor user experience and does not solve the underlying issue.

scenario: A front-end team deploys a new version of their JavaScript bundle. The old bundle is cached by browsers and a CDN with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400`. Users still see the old version.
prompt: What caching strategy would prevent this problem?

options.text: Use Cache-Control: no-store for all JavaScript files
Include a content hash in the filename (e.g. app.3f8a.js) and cache with max-age=31536000, immutable. The HTML page references the new filename.
Set max-age=0 so every request hits the origin
Use PUT instead of GET to fetch the bundle

explanation: Content-hashed filenames change when the code changes, so the browser requests the new URL (cache miss) and caches it for a long time. The HTML page (served with a short max-age or no-cache) references the new filename. (a) and (c) eliminate caching entirely, increasing load and latency. (d) PUT is for writing, not reading.

scenario: An API returns user profile data. The profile changes infrequently (maybe once a month). You want browsers to cache it but not serve stale data after an update.

options.text: Cache-Control: public, max-age=2592000 (30 days)
Cache-Control: private, no-cache with an ETag. The browser caches but revalidates on each use; the server returns 304 if unchanged.
Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=2592000

explanation: private keeps user data out of shared caches (CDNs). no-cache with ETag revalidation ensures the browser always checks for updates, but avoids re-downloading the body when nothing changed (304). (a) and (d) are public and could leak user data to shared caches; also, a 30-day max-age serves stale data after an update. (c) Works but wastes bandwidth by always re-downloading.

prompt: Which of the following HTTP methods are **idempotent**? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE

explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are all idempotent: repeating them produces the same result. POST is not idempotent: repeating it may create multiple resources. (b) is the exception because each POST can have a different side effect.
